title: Why Semantic HTML Matters 🧱
description: Discover how proper HTML structure is the most powerful accessibility tool you have.

slides.title: HTML: The Foundation of the Accessibility Tree 🌳
slides.content:
## Every element has a meaning

When you use a `<button>`, browsers know it's a button. They give it an **implicit role**, keyboard support, and an accessible name automatically.

* **Semantic HTML** = using the right element for the job.
* It's free accessibility – no extra code needed.

Think of it like building with labelled Lego bricks. If you use a roof brick as a wall, the structure still stands – but it's confusing.

quizData.question: What does a `<button>` element provide automatically?

options.text: Keyboard focusability and a role of 'button'

quizData.explanation: Native buttons are focusable, trigger on Enter/Space, and are announced as 'button' by screen readers.

slides.title: Semantic vs. Non‑Semantic
slides.content: Left: semantic. Right: div‑soup. Can you spot the difference?

quizData.question: Why is a `<div>` with an `onclick` not a good button?

options.text: It's not focusable by default and has no button role

quizData.explanation: Divs are not in the tab order and lack the button role, so keyboard and screen reader users can't interact with them.

slides.title: The Accessibility Tree in Action 🌲
slides.content:
The browser converts your HTML into an **accessibility tree** – a simplified version for assistive tech.

* Semantic elements pass their meaning directly into the tree.
* `<nav>` → role="navigation"
* `<main>` → role="main"
* `<h1>` → role="heading" + level 1

Using non‑semantic tags like `<div>` means you must manually add ARIA – which is error‑prone.

slides.title: The First Rule of ARIA 🚫
slides.content:
## Don't use ARIA if you can use a native HTML element

ARIA can fix gaps, but native HTML is always more robust. Always start with semantic HTML.
